units.title: Modern Chinese Art: Finding New Paths
units.intro: In the early 20th century, facing the impact of Western art, Chinese painters tried different ways to 'modernise' Chinese painting.

lessons.title: The Lingnan School's Innovations
cards: The Lingnan School (嶺南畫派) arose in Guangdong in the early 20th century. Its founders, Gao Jianfu (高劍父), Gao Qifeng (高奇峰) and Chen Shuren (陳樹人), are known as the 'Two Gaos and One Chen'.
Gao Jianfu (高劍父) and Chen Shuren (陳樹人) first studied painting under Ju Lian (居廉); Gao Qifeng (高奇峰) learned from his elder brother Gao Jianfu. All three later studied in Japan.
They called for 'blending Chinese and Western, uniting old and new', painting new subjects such as aeroplanes, tanks and other modern things.
In technique, they valued 'water-splashing and powder-splashing' (撞水撞粉), which makes flower-and-bird colours look moist and luminous.
The Lingnan School (嶺南畫派) deeply influenced Hong Kong. Painters such as Chao Shao-an (趙少昂) brought it to Hong Kong and developed it further.

quiz.question: Who is NOT one of the Lingnan School's 'Two Gaos and One Chen'?
quiz.explain: Xu Beihong followed the path of realism and was not a founder of the Lingnan School.

quiz.question: What did the Lingnan School advocate?
options: Blending Chinese and Western, uniting old and new
quiz.answer: Blending Chinese and Western, uniting old and new
quiz.explain: They wanted to keep the brush and ink of Chinese painting while taking in foreign techniques and new subjects.

quiz.question: The Lingnan technique that makes colours moist and luminous is called 'water-splashing and ____'.
quiz.explain: 'Water-splashing and powder-splashing' was developed by Ju Lian and taken up by the Lingnan School.

quiz.question: In which country did Lingnan School painters study and pick up new techniques?
quiz.explain: Gao Jianfu and others studied in Japan, absorbing Japanese painting and Western realist techniques.

lessons.title: Xu Beihong and Realism
cards: Xu Beihong (徐悲鴻, 1895–1953) studied in France at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, learning Western academic drawing and oil painting.
He believed Chinese painting needed 'reform', and argued that Western realist drawing should be the foundation for depicting form.
His most famous subject is galloping horses, painted in ink with accurate anatomy to show strength and speed.
Major works include the oil painting Tian Heng and His Five Hundred Followers (《田橫五百士》), which uses a historical story to express national integrity.
After 1949 he became the first president of the Central Academy of Fine Arts (中央美術學院). His realist teaching system shaped Chinese art education for many years.

quiz.question: What is Xu Beihong's most famous ink-painting subject?
quiz.explain: He used realist knowledge of anatomy to paint horses, with bold brushwork and accurate structure.

quiz.question: What did Xu Beihong say should be the foundation of form in Chinese painting?
quiz.explain: He believed drawing was the foundation of all visual art.

quiz.question: Match each work to its type
options: Tian Heng and His Five Hundred Followers
quiz.explain: Xu Beihong worked in both oil and ink.

quiz.question: After 1949, Xu Beihong became the first president of which school?
quiz.explain: His realist teaching system spread from there.

lessons.title: Lin Fengmian's Fusion
cards: Lin Fengmian (林風眠, 1900–1991) studied in France and was strongly influenced by Western modernism, such as Fauvism and Cubism.
In 1928 he founded the National Academy of Art (國立藝術院) in Hangzhou, today's China Academy of Art, promoting 'harmonising Chinese and Western art'.
He often used square compositions, combining ink, watercolour and rich colour. His subjects include ladies, still lifes, egrets and autumn scenes.
His students included Wu Guanzhong (吳冠中), Zao Wou-Ki (趙無極) and Chu Teh-Chun (朱德群), who all became important modern artists.
In his later years he settled in Hong Kong, where he kept creating art until his death.

quiz.question: Where did Lin Fengmian found the National Academy of Art?
quiz.explain: Founded in 1928, it is today's China Academy of Art.

quiz.question: Which of these was NOT a student of Lin Fengmian?
quiz.explain: Gao Jianfu was a founder of the Lingnan School and older than Lin Fengmian.

quiz.question: Which composition format is common in Lin Fengmian's work?
quiz.explain: The square format broke away from traditional Chinese scroll formats and is close to the Western idea of a framed picture.

quiz.question: Lin Fengmian promoted '____ Chinese and Western art'.
quiz.explain: He wanted to combine the spirit of Chinese art with modern Western forms.

lessons.title: Wu Guanzhong and Formal Beauty
cards: Wu Guanzhong (吳冠中, 1919–2010) studied under Lin Fengmian (林風眠) at the National Hangzhou Academy of Art, then went to study in Paris.
He valued 'formal beauty' (形式美): dots, lines, planes and colours are beautiful in themselves, so a painting need not be realistic.
He often painted Jiangnan (江南) water towns: white walls, black tiles, curving lines and dots of colour, in simple, rhythmic pictures.
In 1992 he published 'Brush and Ink Equal Zero' (〈筆墨等於零〉), arguing that brush and ink must serve the picture and are worthless on their own. It caused huge debate.
He painted in both oil and ink, aiming to 'give oil painting a national character and modernise Chinese painting'.

quiz.question: What did Wu Guanzhong paint most often?
quiz.explain: White walls and black tiles provide the formal elements of dot, line and plane.

quiz.question: In 1992 Wu Guanzhong published an essay called 'Brush and Ink Equal ____'.
quiz.explain: He argued that brush and ink are worthless apart from the picture, which sparked a big debate.

quiz.question: What does 'formal beauty' mainly emphasise?
options: The beauty of dots, lines, planes and colour themselves
quiz.answer: The beauty of dots, lines, planes and colour themselves
quiz.explain: Formal beauty focuses on the picture's elements and how they are organised.

quiz.question: Who was Wu Guanzhong's teacher?
quiz.explain: He studied under Lin Fengmian at the National Hangzhou Academy of Art.

lessons.title: Zao Wou-Ki and Abstraction
cards: Zao Wou-Ki (趙無極, 1920–2013) studied under Lin Fengmian (林風眠) at the National Hangzhou Academy of Art, and moved to Paris in 1948.
Early on he was inspired by Paul Klee (保羅·克利), and symbols like oracle bone script (甲骨文) appeared in his paintings.
He later developed lyrical abstraction: large fields of colour and flowing brushstrokes that evoke landscapes, light and the universe.
Many works are titled by completion date, such as June–October 1985 (《1985年6月-10月》), so viewers don't read them as specific subjects.
In 2002 he was elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts (法蘭西藝術院) in France. He is a leading figure of abstract art fusing East and West.

quiz.question: Which city did Zao Wou-Ki move to in 1948?
quiz.explain: In Paris he encountered modern Western art and developed his abstract style.

quiz.question: Which Western artist inspired Zao Wou-Ki early in his career?
quiz.explain: Klee's symbols and lines inspired him to add symbols like oracle bone script.

quiz.question: How did Zao Wou-Ki title many of his works?
quiz.explain: Date titles make viewers focus on colour and space, not a specific subject.

quiz.question: Match each artist to their style
quiz.explain: All three wanted to modernise Chinese art, but in different ways.

quiz.question: How does Zao Wou-Ki's work show a fusion of East and West?
options: Using oil paint to express the mood of Chinese landscape
Only copying ancient paintings in ink
quiz.answer: Using oil paint to express the mood of Chinese landscape
quiz.explain: A Western medium combined with Eastern ideas of space and qiyun (spirit resonance).

units.title: Hong Kong Art and Identity
units.intro: From New Ink to contemporary practice, Hong Kong artists respond to the city, identity and collecting spaces—aligned with CCCKLC F.6 themes and museum visits (HK Palace Museum, Xubaizhai).

lessons.title: New Ink: Lui Shou-kwan and Wucius Wong
cards: Lui Shou-kwan (1919–1975) was a key force in Hong Kong New Ink, refining landscape into bold ink masses and voids with a Zen, abstract lean.
Rather than only copying models, he used modern composition and simplified form so ink could speak about mind-states, not just scenery.
Wucius Wong, inspired by Lui, joined design-like structure to ink, stressing order, layering and geometry.
New Ink helped post-war Hong Kong build a local modern ink language—an important chapter of artistic identity.
(Pending teacher review) Use a visual diary to note how void and ink mass can carry emotion.

quiz.question: Hong Kong’s modern ink movement linked to Lui is usually called?
quiz.explain: Lui is a major New Ink pioneer in Hong Kong.

quiz.question: A formal trait often seen in Lui’s work is?
quiz.explain: Abstracted landscape with breathing empty space.

quiz.question: Wucius Wong’s ink often stresses design-like ＿＿ and layers.
quiz.explain: He brings design thinking into ink.

quiz.question: Why does New Ink matter for HK identity?
options: It built a local modern ink language
quiz.answer: It built a local modern ink language

lessons.title: Luis Chan’s Surreal Hong Kong
cards: Luis Chan (1905–1995) began with more naturalistic views and portraits; from the 1960s his art turned fantastical and surreal.
Bright colour, naïve forms and dream logic turn Hong Kong hills and harbour into imagined worlds.
Humour and folk-like play challenge the idea that Hong Kong art must only document reality.
For DSE students he models surreal strategies for “everyday city + inner feeling”.
(Pending teacher review) Maps to CCCKLC’s “explore surreal life” aim.

quiz.explain: City and hills become dream scenes.

lessons.title: Contemporary HK identity: Pak, Lee Kit, Wilson Shieh
cards: Pak Sheung Chuen uses conceptual gestures and everyday materials to make pressure of housing and city space thinkable.
Lee Kit builds quiet installations with painting, cloth, projection and domestic objects—private, fragile moments.
Wilson Shieh paints contemporary figures in gongbi colour; faces may be blank or role-like, probing identity and gender.
Concept, spatial sensing and figuration—all ask who we are and how we live here.
(Pending teacher review) Ties to CCCKLC “Self…society” and role-taking.

lessons.title: Museums and local collections: HKPM & Xubaizhai
cards: The Hong Kong Palace Museum stages exhibitions tied to Palace Museum culture—useful for material culture and aesthetics.
The Xubaizhai Collection at the Hong Kong Museum of Art centres Chinese painting and calligraphy for literati study.
A visit is observation practice: composition, colophons, seals, mounting and display narratives.
CCCKLC F.6 links these visits to self-review and portfolio; keep a visual diary of questions.

units.title: Introduction to Western Modernism
units.intro: From Impressionism to abstraction, then a bridge to postmodern identity, Cindy Sherman and the YBA—matching CCCKLC needs.

lessons.title: Impressionism: Monet and van Gogh
cards: Impressionists prized outdoor light, visible brushwork and fleeting colour over polished academic finish.
Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise (1872) and Water Lilies explore changing light and reflection.
Vincent van Gogh pushed high chroma and swirling stroke so touch itself carries feeling.
Both unsettled “likeness alone” as the only standard and opened doors to modernism.
(Pending teacher review) A light link to ink “stroke as feeling” can wait for U5.

lessons.title: Fauvism and Cubism: Matisse and Picasso
cards: Henri Matisse and the Fauves used intense, non-natural colour and simplified shape.
Pablo Picasso and Braque built Cubism by fracturing forms into multi-view planes.
Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (1907) is an early Cubist landmark breaking stable perspective.
Modernism could reinvent seeing through colour or through structural analysis.
(Pending teacher review) Pair with Tate “human figure” resources.

lessons.title: Paths to abstraction: Kandinsky, Mondrian, Rothko
cards: Wassily Kandinsky argued colour and shape can free themselves from objects; Concerning the Spiritual in Art was influential.
Piet Mondrian’s Neo-Plasticism uses horizontals, verticals and primary colours for balance.
Mark Rothko’s colour-field paintings immerse viewers in soft-edged fields of feeling.
Abstraction is organised meaning—not “anything goes”.
(Pending teacher review) Cross-link Wu Guanzhong / Zao Wou-Ki later.

lessons.title: Postmodern identity: Sherman and the YBA
cards: Postmodern work often questions “authentic identity” and originality via appropriation and role-play.
Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Stills (1977–1980) stages typed female roles to probe gaze and representation.
The YBA emerged in 1990s Britain; Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin became widely known for startling materials and autobiographical strategies.
This bridge lesson supports CCCKLC role-taking: “Reappear someone in Chinese context”.
(Pending teacher review) Extend with Tate “changed identity” / “human figure”.

units.title: Contemporary Chinese Art
units.intro: Bridge from Xu Beihong and Qi Baishi into Xu Bing, Political Pop, installation/performance and video—aligned with F.5 Art Talk and global contemporary views.

lessons.title: Bridge: Xu Beihong and Qi Baishi toward today
cards: Xu Beihong championed academic drawing; horses and history subjects tied structure to national meaning.
Qi Baishi brought folk-flavoured birds, fish and insects into modern viewership.
Later artists inherit these “modern classics” while facing globalisation and new media.
Seeing realist pedagogy and folk wit first makes later refusals and appropriations clearer.
(Pending teacher review) Detail on Xu also sits in U1.

lessons.title: Xu Bing: writing, concept, calligraphy currents
cards: Book from the Sky (1980s) prints invented pseudo-characters, unsettling trust in writing.
Language, reading and cultural misreading link conceptual art to calligraphic tradition.
F.5 Art Talk pairs Xu Bing with contemporary Chinese calligraphy currents and global art.
Students may translate the idea of a broken writing system into school, net or dialect barriers.
(Pending teacher review) Transform the concept—do not only copy pseudo-glyphs for marks.

cards: Wang Guangyi’s Great Criticism-type works juxtapose propaganda imagery with consumer logos.
Yue Minjun’s laughing figures and Fang Lijun’s bald heads are discussed in Cynical Realism contexts.
They respond to memory, consumption and mood after Reform—not “pretty painting” alone.
Compare carefully with Warhol’s mass-image tactics (U5); contexts differ.

lessons.title: Installation, performance and video
cards: Cai Guo-Qiang is known for gunpowder drawings and explosion events—ephemeral mark and spectacle.
Zhang Huan and others use the body as medium under social gaze.
Zhang Peili is a key early video figure; Yang Fudong works with cinematic time; Cao Fei explores virtual worlds and subcultures.
New media lets the work be process, event or virtual space.

lessons.title: Symbols: literati cues meet today (U6 preview)
cards: Ming–Qing literati painting uses birds, strange rocks, colophons and brush habits as moral/feeling signs; Bada Shanren’s creatures are often read with loyalist anguish.
Wu School figures such as Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming stress poetry–calligraphy–painting unity; Xu Wei and Chen Chun push freer xieyi ink.
Contemporaries may reuse or deliberately misalign these signs for present issues.
CCCKLC asks students to read colour/pattern/painting symbols beside postmodern practice.
